[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and let
$1\le i\le n-2$. Put
$$W_{i,i+1}:=\langle s_i,s_{i+1}\rangle\le S_n,\qquad R^{W_{i,i+1}}:=R^{s_i}\cap R^{s_{i+1}},$$
the parabolic subgroup generated by the two adjacent simple reflections and its
invariant ring. The two generators act as adjacent transpositions on the three indicated
coordinates and fix every other coordinate, so their restriction is an
isomorphism $W_{i,i+1}\cong S_3$ by the generation clause of
[[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]]; the subgroup permutes the three coordinates
$x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ and fixes every other coordinate, so $R^{W_{i,i+1}}$ is
the ring of polynomials in $x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ that are invariant under all
permutations of the three, with all other $x_j$ adjoined as invariants. The
element
$$w_{i,i+1}:=s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}\in W_{i,i+1}$$

$$B_{i,i+1,i}:=R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R(3),$$

$(R^{W_{i,i+1}},R)$-bimodule $R$, with the total grading of the tensor product
shifted by the external shift $(3)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]], that is
$$(3)=\{-3\},\qquad (B_{i,i+1,i})_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R\bigr)_{d+3} \ \ \text{in the convention } M(r)_d=M_{d+r}.$$

$$B_{\underline{i,i+1,i}}=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i =R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\otimes_{R^{s_{i+1}}}R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(3)$$

consumers.claim:
**Soergel graphs.** Fix $n\ge2$ and the type-A realization of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], so the colors are the
simple reflections $s_1,\ldots,s_{n-1}$, with $m_{st}=3$ for $|s-t|=1$ and
$m_{st}=2$ for $|s-t|>1$. A *Soergel graph* is an isotopy class of decorated
graphs embedded in the planar strip $\mathbb R\times[0,1]$, as in
Elias–Williamson, Definition 5.1: edges are colored by simple reflections and may
meet the bottom boundary $\mathbb R\times\{0\}$ and the top boundary
$\mathbb R\times\{1\}$ in colored boundary points; the decorations are boxes
labelled by homogeneous elements $f\in R$, and the vertices are of three types,
with the degrees of Elias–Williamson, Definition 5.1:

1. univalent vertices (*dots*), degree $+1$;
2. trivalent vertices, all three adjoining edges of one color, degree $-1$;
3. $2m_{st}$-valent vertices, the adjoining edges alternating between two colors
   $s\ne t$ with $m_{st}<\infty$, degree $0$; in type $A$ this is a $4$-valent
   vertex when $|s-t|>1$ and a $6$-valent vertex when $|s-t|=1$.

The degree of a graph is the sum of the degrees of its vertices and boxes; a
graph with bottom boundary $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ and top boundary $(j_1,\ldots,j_s)$
has boundary dots of those colors and is read from bottom to top. Composing
graphs by vertical juxtaposition and tensoring them by horizontal juxtaposition
is the usual pasting of boundary graphs.

**The category $D$.** Let $D$ (also written $D_n$) denote the $\mathbb Q$-linear
monoidal category of Elias–Williamson, Definition 5.2, in this type-A case:
objects are the words $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ in the alphabet
$\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ — we also write $B_{\underline i}$ for the object, in the
notation of [[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]] — with monoidal structure
given by concatenation and with the empty word as unit; the hom space
$\operatorname{Hom}_D(\underline i,\underline j)$ is the free $\mathbb Q$-module
on the Soergel graphs with bottom boundary $\underline i$ and top boundary
$\underline j$, graded by graph degree and with **degree-zero** composites, modulo
the homogeneous relations of the source, which in type $A$ are:

1. the polynomial relations (5.1) and (5.2) of Elias–Williamson §5.1, which slide
   boxes labelled by $f\in R$ across strands at the cost of the appropriate
   action of the Coxeter group and the Demazure operator, with the root labelling
   the dot on a strand of color $s$;
2. the one-color relations (5.3)–(5.5) of Elias–Williamson §5.1: the Frobenius
   relations among dots and trivalent vertices of a single color and the
   needle relation (5.5): a one-color loop attached at a trivalent vertex
   to a single strand is zero;
3. the two-color relations of Elias–Williamson §§5.2–5.3, in the two parities;
   for distant colors ($m_{st}=2$) the $4$-valent vertex is an interchange
   isomorphism, and for adjacent colors ($m_{st}=3$) the $6$-valent vertex
   satisfies the Jones–Wenzl relations, including the two ways of reading the
   relation that resolve the two triple products
   $B_iB_{i+1}B_i\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_i$ and
   $B_{i+1}B_iB_{i+1}\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_{i+1}$ of
   [[thm-rank-two-type-a-soergel-bimodule-decompositions]];
4. the three-color relations of Elias–Williamson §§5.4–5.5, which in type $A$
   are: the $A_1\times I_2(m)$ relation (5.8) for a triple of colours consisting
   of two adjacent colours together with a third colour distant from both; its
   special case (5.9) for three pairwise distant colours; and the $A_3$
   *Zamolodchikov relation* (5.10) on three consecutive colours. The $B_3$ and
   $H_3$ relations (5.11)–(5.12) of the source are not part of the type-$A$
   presentation, and Elias–Williamson's Definition 5.2 lists all of (5.8),
   (5.9) and (5.10) before the definition is complete.

For type $A$ the same presentation is enumerated, with all generators, degrees
and local relations, in Elias–Khovanov, Definition 3.8 and §3.4 (relations
(3.1)–(3.37)); the indexing there is $S_{n+1}$ with colors $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and
polynomial ring in $n+1$ variables of degree $2$, and its internal shift is
translated to the library by $M\{-1\}=M(1)$, as on this page. The Karoubi
envelope $\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ is the idempotent completion of the additive
graded closure of $D$, using degree-zero idempotents and morphisms there.

**The candidate bimodule functor.** Let $\mathcal F:D\to R\text{-Bim}$ be the
assignment that sends a word $\underline i$ to the Bott–Samelson bimodule
$B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ of
[[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]] and a graph to a bimodule map by the
following images on the generating vertices, all of which are the maps displayed
in Elias–Williamson, p. 5, written here in the library's shifts and with
$\alpha_s$ and $\partial_s(f)=(f-sf)/\alpha_s$:

1. the degree-$+1$ dot $B_s\to R$ ↦ the map $f\otimes g\mapsto fg$;
2. the degree-$+1$ dot $R\to B_s$ ↦ the map $1\mapsto\tfrac12(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s)$;
3. the degree-$-1$ trivalent vertices ↦ the maps
   $1\otimes g\otimes1\mapsto\partial_sg\otimes1$ and $1\otimes1\mapsto1\otimes1\otimes1$;
4. a box labelled by homogeneous $f\in R$ ↦ multiplication by $f$ in the region
   of the tensor product where the box lies, that is, the $R$-bimodule structure
   of the corresponding Bott–Samelson bimodule;
5. a $4$-valent vertex of two distant colors ↦ the interchange isomorphism
   $B_i\otimes_RB_j\to B_j\otimes_RB_i$ of
   [[lem-distant-soergel-generators-commute]];
6. a $6$-valent vertex of two adjacent colors ↦ the unique degree-zero
   bimodule map between the two alternating reduced-word products that sends
   their $1$-tensor to the $1$-tensor, as specified for a $2m$-valent vertex in
   Elias–Williamson §§5.2–5.3 (and given explicitly by Libedinsky). It factors
   through the common summand $B_{i,i+1,i}$ of the two triple products in
   [[thm-rank-two-type-a-soergel-bimodule-decompositions]]; the existence of
   that summand alone does not specify the map's scalar.

**Status.** The assignment $\mathcal F$ is a *candidate*: this item defines its
values on generators only, and no functoriality is asserted here. That the values
respect the relations, so that $\mathcal F$ is a graded monoidal functor, is the
content of the next item on this page; the functor is not asserted to be an
equivalence before the double-leaves items.

$$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
with the pair ordered so that the multiplicity vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the
Bruhat order; in particular the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture's multiplicity
statement holds for every dominant regular integral weight, with the same
combinatorial answer.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a dominant regular
integral weight $\lambda$ of the complex type-$A$ Lie algebra and the standard
parabolic $\mathfrak p_J$, with reductive Levi $\mathfrak l_J$ and longest
Levi Weyl element $w_J$
([[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]]). The
$\mathfrak p_J$-dominant weights in this regular block are exactly
$y\cdot\lambda$ for $y\in{}^JW$. Write
$\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)=M_{\mathfrak p}(y\cdot\lambda)$,
$L(x\cdot\lambda)$ and $P^J(x\cdot\lambda)$ for its generalized standards,
simples and projective covers
([[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]]). Then for
$x,y\in{}^JW$,
$$[\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]=(P^J(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}P_{uy,x}(1)=n_{y,x}(1).$$

These are the antispherical sign coefficients, with support $y\le x$ and
diagonal $1$. The precise character/Grothendieck identity supplying the
formula is
$$\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}\operatorname{ch}\Delta(uy\cdot\lambda).$$

For the same highest weights in the antidominant base
$\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}=w_0\cdot\lambda$, the actual longest-left label is
$z=yw_0$, since $y\cdot\lambda=z\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$.
Its shortest-left encoding is $a=\mathrm{lf}(y):=w_Jyw_0\in{}^JW$, so the
weight in that encoding is $(w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$, not
$a\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$. With $b=\mathrm{lf}(x)$, the reindexed matrix is
$$\widetilde N_{a,b}:=n_{\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(a),\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(b)}(1)=n_{w_Jaw_0,\,w_Jbw_0}(1).$$
It is the same multiplicity matrix with both indices permuted and has reversed
support in the transported order. It is not in general $n_{a,b}(1)$.
Every label retains its explicit dot-baseweight.
The highest-weight category theorem applies also to singular integral
parabolic blocks, but this ordinary regular KL matrix formula assumes the
ambient central character is regular. No singular/parabolic category
equivalence, grading or Koszul duality is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work in the type-$A$
root datum $W=S_n$ of the page's Hecke module and ordinary multiplicity
theorem. Let $(\lambda,\mu)$ be as in [[lem-facet-tensor-weight-exclusion]]
with $J=J(\mu)$, so $\mathcal O_\mu$ is the singular integral block of
[[def-singular-integral-category-o-block-and-stabilizer]] with labels
normalized by the minimal right coset representatives $W^J$, and let $w_0$ be
the longest element of $W$. Then for all $y,w\in W^J$,
$$[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=P_{yw_0,\,ww_0}(1),$$
the value at $q=1$ of the ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomial attached to the
pair $(yw_0,ww_0)$ in the classical normalization of
[[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]].
Equivalently, put $k(w)=w_0^Jw^{-1}w_0\in{}^JW$. Then
$$[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=m_{k(y),k(w)}(1).$$
This is the spherical family. The antispherical family instead governs the
genuine regular parabolic locally finite category with dominant labels;
changing to an opposite positive system does not identify the two families.
In particular all singular multiplicities are computable from the ordinary
Kazhdan--Lusztig coefficients of $S_n$, and no individual polynomial
coefficients beyond the value at one occur.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for every $w\in W$ the class of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ in the
Grothendieck group, equivalently its formal character, is
$$[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda),$$
where $q'_{x,w}$ are the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients of
[[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] ($Q'=P^{-1}$, $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$
for $x<w$, $q'_{w,w}=1$) and the sum is supported on $x\ge w$. Equivalently, in
the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ the
formula is the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum
$$\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda).$$
The coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ are the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of
$(P_{y,z}(1))$, given by the finite signed chain sum of products of
$P_{y,z}(1)$; they are integers that may be negative. They specialize to
ordinary Bruhat Möbius values on intervals where every comparable-pair
Kazhdan–Lusztig value is $1$, but not in general. Only the value at $q=1$
occurs.

[[lem-residue-casimir-operators-give-local-affine-hecke-actions]].

The first-$i$ image in its central fibre is $\mathrm{Mat}_{i!}(Z_{i,r})$, where
$$Z_{i,r}=\mathbb C[c_1,\dots,c_i]/(h_{r-i+1},\dots,h_r)$$

complete-intersection Frobenius ring of dimension $\binom{r}{i}$ with
one-dimensional socle. Divided residue functors and the complementary-idempotent
restriction have the corresponding simple head and socle.

Consequently $e_iL(A)$ and $f_iL(A)$ are either $0$ or self-dual
indecomposables with simple isomorphic head and socle labelled
$\tilde e_iA$, respectively $\tilde f_iA$. Vanishing is exactly the absence of
the corresponding crystal edge. This retains the complete residue-translation
crystal claim, not only its $K_0$ action.

Assume inherited AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for the invoked cyclotomic PBW/Skryabin and category-O single-block suppliers; the explicit finite spectral and centre computations below introduce no additional choice.

Fix a nonempty set $I\subseteq\mathbb Z$ of consecutive integers (possibly all of
$\mathbb Z$ or half-infinite), put $I^+:=I\cup(I+1)$, fix a level $l\ge1$ and an
integral multicharge $m_1\ge\cdots\ge m_l$ with $m_j\in I^+$, and let
$\Lambda=\sum_{j=1}^{l}\Lambda_{m_j}\in P^+$ be the corresponding dominant
integral weight. Throughout, the ground field is $\mathbb C$ and the degree-$d$
degenerate cyclotomic Hecke algebra is defined by $H_0(m):=\mathbb C$ and,
for $d\ge1$, by the algebra $H_d(m)$ of
[[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]]: the quotient of the degenerate
affine Hecke algebra by the relation $(x_1-m_1)\cdots(x_1-m_l)=0$, with
$\mathbb C$-basis $\{x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w\}$ over $0\le r_i<l$, $w\in S_d$,
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}H_d(m)=l^d d!$ for $d\ge1$. At $d=0$ the basis is the
singleton empty word and the dimension is $1$; there is no $x_1$ and no
cyclotomic relation to impose. The $x_1,\dots,x_d$ commute pairwise in every
positive degree.

**(1) Joint spectral idempotents and content idempotents.** For
$i=(i_1,\dots,i_d)\in\mathbb Z^d$ let $e(i)\in H_d(m)$ be the joint polynomial
spectral idempotent of $x_1,\dots,x_d$ that projects onto the generalized joint
eigenspace with generalized eigenvalues $i_1,\dots,i_d$; these idempotents are
those of [[def-stable-range-and-block-idempotent-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
they lie in the commutative subalgebra generated by $x_1,\dots,x_d$, are
mutually orthogonal, sum to the identity of $H_d(m)$, and all but finitely many
are zero. For $\alpha\in Q^+$ with $d=\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$ put

$$I_\alpha:=\{\,i\in I^d\ :\ \textstyle\sum_{r=1}^{d}\alpha_{i_r}=\alpha\,\},\qquad e_\alpha:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}e(i)\in H_d(m),\qquad H^\Lambda_\alpha:=e_\alpha H_d(m).$$

Because $I_\alpha$ is finite (so only finitely many nonzero $e(i)$ occur in it),
$e_\alpha$ is an idempotent of $H_d(m)$, nonzero or zero, and $H^\Lambda_\alpha$
is a finite-dimensional algebra with identity $e_\alpha$. Its (finite
dimensional, unital) left modules are exactly the $H_d(m)$-modules on which
$e_\alpha$ acts as the identity.

**(2) The supported degree and the tower.** The **degree-$d$ supported tower
algebra** is $f_{I,d}H_d(m)$ with $f_{I,d}:=\sum_{i\in I^d}e(i)$; for
$I\ne\mathbb Z$ this is in general a proper central cut of the whole degree-$d$
algebra $H_d(m)$, and no equality with $H_d(m)$ is asserted. The **tower** is

$$H^\Lambda:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q^+}H^\Lambda_\alpha .$$

It is a unital algebra when $I$ is finite and a locally unital algebra in
general; the ambient tower inclusion is the degree-raising embedding
$\iota\colon H_d(m)\hookrightarrow H_{d+1}(m)$ of
[[def-hecke-induction-and-restriction-functors-on-degenerate-cyclotomic-blocks]].
At level $0$ the tower is concentrated in degree $0$: $H^\Lambda_0=\mathbb C$
and $H^\Lambda_d=0$ for $d>0$.

**(3) Grothendieck groups and the Cartan pairing.** For each $\alpha$ let
$D(A)$ range over representatives of the simple finite-dimensional
$H^\Lambda_\alpha$-modules and $Y(A)\twoheadrightarrow D(A)$ over their
projective covers. The **module Grothendieck group** $G_0(H^\Lambda_\alpha)$ is
the Grothendieck group $G_0$ of the category of finite-dimensional
$H^\Lambda_\alpha$-modules ([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]])
and the **split projective group** $K_0(H^\Lambda_\alpha)$ is the split
Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional projective modules
([[def-split-grothendieck-group-of-an-additive-category]]); both are taken block
by block and then summed over $\alpha\in Q^+$. The **Cartan pairing**

$$\langle-,-\rangle\colon K_0(H^\Lambda)\times G_0(H^\Lambda)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \langle[P],[M]\rangle:=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{H^\Lambda}(P,M),$$

is the object-level Hom pairing of
